summary: White space is radio spectrum assigned to a use but unused at certain places and times. This document states the problem for a protocol to access a database of white-space information, then gives use cases and requirements for it.

eli5.summary: Some radio channels sit empty in some places. This explains why we need a lookup to learn which ones are free to use.

questions: what is paws white space database protocol
tv white space database access requirements
how do white space devices find available spectrum
subtitle: Requirements for accessing a database of available radio spectrum

tldr.problem: Radio spectrum assigned to a primary user (like TV broadcasters) sits unused in many places and times. Secondary users could use this white space without interfering, but they need a way to learn which frequencies are available at their location before transmitting. Different countries regulate white space use differently, so a global, flexible protocol is needed.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6953 specifies requirements for a database query protocol (PAWS, later defined in other RFCs) that white-space devices use to query a database with their location and characteristics, receive a list of available frequencies and maximum power levels, and report back which frequencies they choose to use. The protocol must support master devices querying on behalf of slave devices and must be flexible enough for different regulatory rule sets.
tldr.outcome: This is an informational requirements document. The actual PAWS protocol was developed afterward based on these requirements. White-space spectrum remains underutilized in practice, though the protocol enables opportunistic spectrum sharing in countries that permit it.

today: RFC 6953 is an informational document that has not been obsoleted. It provided the requirements basis for the PAWS (Protocol to Access White-Space) protocol, though white-space spectrum deployment has remained limited in practice outside of test deployments and a few regulatory jurisdictions that permit it.

sections.title: White Space and the Challenge
sections.content:
Wireless spectrum is a limited resource assigned by governments. Even when a frequency band is licensed to a primary user like a TV broadcaster, the same frequency may not be used everywhere at all times. White space is spectrum that is assigned but unused at specific locations and times. A secondary user—perhaps a Wi-Fi hotspot or emergency responder—could use that frequency without interfering with the primary user if it knew where the white space exists.

The RFC explains that knowing which frequencies are available depends on both location and time, and varies by country and regulatory regime. Rather than require different databases and protocols for each country, the RFC proposes a single, global protocol with a flexible data model.
sections.eli5: Some radio channels are officially assigned but sit empty in many places. Devices could use empty channels without breaking anything, but they need a lookup table to know which ones are free.

sections.title: Devices, Databases, and Discovery
sections.content:
The protocol involves master devices (which query a database directly and have internet connectivity) and slave devices (which may not have internet access and ask the master to query on their behalf). The master must discover the address of a white-space database it can trust, either through a discovery service or by pre-configuration. After discovering a database, the master may register with it, providing owner and device information.

The RFC notes that multiple databases may serve the same area in some countries (like the US), so a master may need to discover and select among several.
sections.eli5: A main device talks to a central database of available channels. Smaller devices can ask the main device to look things up for them. There may be multiple databases in the same area.

sections.title: Queries, Responses, and Usage Reporting
sections.content:
The master device sends a query including its geolocation, device identification, antenna characteristics (height, gain, radiation pattern), and maximum power it can transmit. The query may also include information for one or more slave devices. The database responds with a list of available frequencies, maximum power levels allowed, and schedules (start and stop times) when each frequency is available. The master may then send an acknowledgment back to the database indicating which frequencies and power levels it actually chose, on behalf of itself and any slave devices.

The data model must be flexible enough to handle different spectral definitions: some bands are defined as channels (named allocations), while others are defined as frequency ranges (low to high frequency). It must support different device types: fixed installations, portable devices, and mobile devices.
sections.eli5: A device sends: where it is, what it can do, and how powerful it is. The database replies: these channels are free, you can use up to this power. The device confirms back: I'm using these channels. Definitions must work worldwide.

sections.title: Common Use Cases
sections.content: The RFC describes five main use cases. Master-slave networks are common in rural or densely packed scenarios where a master device controls spectrum for one or more slave devices. Offloading uses white space to unload traffic from congested primary networks. Backhaul uses white-space links to carry internet traffic to areas without good connectivity. Emergency networks use white space to quickly set up communication during disasters. Local TV broadcast uses white space to send video to portable receivers at events.
sections.eli5: One device manages a group. Traffic gets rerouted to empty channels. Far-away places get internet via white-space links. Disasters need fast networks. Events broadcast video locally.

sections.title: Protocol and Data Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC specifies detailed data model requirements: the protocol must support geolocation with uncertainty, device identification and characteristics, antenna parameters, owner information, spectrum availability with schedules and power limits, and reporting of selected frequencies. Protocol requirements include database discovery, registration, available-spectrum queries and responses, spectrum usage acknowledgments, device validation requests, and notification of changes to spectrum availability.

Security is critical: the protocol must authenticate master devices to databases, verify database authenticity, protect message integrity and confidentiality, and support privacy-sensitive handling of location data. The protocol must be globally applicable, spectrum-agnostic, interface-agnostic, and built on flexible, extensible data structures.
sections.eli5: The database needs to know: where a device is, what kind it is, how powerful it is, who owns it. The protocol must let devices register, ask for available channels, report back, and securely verify each other.
